title: Fallacy Catalog
description: A plain, sourced catalog of named logical fallacies for checking real arguments. Each entry gives a standard name, aliases, a category, a short definition, an original example, the conditions that must all be shown from the text before the label applies, legitimate look-alikes that are not the fallacy, whether the fallacy can be detected from the text alone, related entries to choose between, and the published references that list it.

families.name: naturalism
families.rule: Pick the one that matches the step: identifying 'good' with a natural property (naturalistic), a bare is-to-ought step (is-ought), 'natural so good' (appeal to nature), an ought-claim used to settle what is true (moralistic), the outcome of a belief used to settle its truth (consequences).

families.name: ad hominem
families.rule: One label per attack. Use the most specific: circumstances or stake (circumstantial), hypocrisy (tu quoque), motives (appeal to motive), explaining away a view not yet shown wrong (bulverism), pre-emptive (poisoning the well), association (guilt by association), origin (genetic).

families.name: authority and popularity
families.rule: Use one: expertise (authority), fame (celebrity), achievement in another field (accomplishment), numbers (people), a growing trend (bandwagon), age (tradition), newness (novelty), group loyalty (group think), era (chronological snobbery), money (wealth or poverty).

families.name: emotion
families.rule: Use the specific emotion entry if one fits; appeal to emotion only if none does.

families.name: omitted evidence
families.rule: For a passage that leaves out contrary evidence, use suppressed evidence or a more specific text-level entry; the bias entries (confirmation bias, selective attention) are questions only.

families.name: generalization
families.rule: One label per step: rule misapplied to an exception (accident), dropped qualification (secundum quid), too few cases (hasty), exceptions made into a rule (converse accident), stories (anecdotal), vivid case (misleading vividness), biased sample (unrepresentative sample), group image applied to an individual (stereotyping).

families.name: diversion
families.rule: One label per move. Use the most specific; non sequitur and irrelevant conclusion are fallbacks.

families.name: bare assertion
families.rule: Use one: no support at all (ipse dixit), restating against a counterargument (proof by assertion), citing many repetitions or others' silence as evidence (repetition), a stock phrase (cliche), declaring a view absurd without showing it (appeal to the stone), mocking it for a laugh (ridicule), a right to an opinion (entitled), truth said to be relative to the person (subjectivist), refusing to look (willed ignorance), a phrase in place of evidence (proof surrogate).

families.name: causation
families.rule: Use the specific causal entry; false cause only if none fits. Only a correlation is shown: cum hoc. The argument does address causes but misses an obvious third factor: ignoring a common cause. The reverse direction is named and plausible: reversing causation.

families.name: definition and meaning shifts
families.rule: Use one: built-in evaluation (persuasive definition), unannounced new meaning (redefinition), shift after an objection (definitional retreat), shift to exclude a counterexample (no true Scotsman), bold-to-modest switch and back (motte-and-bailey), one word two senses (equivocation).

families.name: circularity
families.rule: Use one: begging the question for the general case; the others when the circle is in an analogy, a label, a question, or a contested doctrine treated as settled.

families.name: ambiguity
families.rule: One word (equivocation), grammar (amphiboly), stress (accent), reach of 'not' or 'all' (scope), word grouping (combination/division of words). When the shifting word is the middle term of a categorical syllogism, report it as equivocation and add '(four terms)'.

families.name: parts and wholes
families.rule: Parts to whole (composition), whole to parts (division), group data to individuals (ecological).

families.name: comparison
families.rule: Use one: a conclusion carried across from one case to another (false analogy), two things called equal (false equivalence), two sides given equal coverage (false balance).

families.name: options and limits
families.rule: Use one per step. No sharp line, so no real difference (line-drawing); a conclusion that trades on a fuzzy term (vagueness).

families.name: ignorance and burden
families.rule: Use one: absence of proof as proof (argument from ignorance), demanding disproof of an unsupported claim (misplaced burden), absence from a source (silence), personal disbelief (incredulity).

families.name: rescuing a claim
families.rule: Use one: an unsupported extra assumption (ad hoc rescue), redefining a group (no true Scotsman), quiet weakening (hedging), raised standard (goalposts), immune to evidence (unfalsifiability), word shift (definitional retreat), bold/modest switch (motte-and-bailey).

families.name: consistency
families.rule: Use the specific entry; inconsistency only if none fits.

families.name: multiple testing
families.rule: Use one per analysis.

families.name: chance
families.rule: Use one per step.

families.name: probability
families.rule: Use one per step. A screening or test result combined with how common the condition is: base-rate fallacy. 'The chance of this evidence if innocent' presented as the chance of innocence: prosecutor's fallacy.

families.name: conditionals
families.rule: Use the exact form; do not tag both a form and its general name.

families.name: syllogisms
families.rule: Name the rule that is broken; use one per syllogism unless two rules are broken. When a term shifts meaning, report it as equivocation and add '(four terms)'.

families.name: quantifiers and modality
families.rule: Use one per step.

families.name: projection
families.rule: Use one: human traits onto animals or things (anthropomorphism), onto lifeless nature (pathetic), abstractions as agents (reification), perception onto the object (mind projection), observer onto subject (psychologist's), word onto object (referential), inner agent (homunculus).

families.name: history
families.rule: Use one per step.

families.name: proportion
families.rule: Use the specific entry; lack of proportion and oversimplification are fallbacks.

families.name: measurement and models
families.rule: Use one per step.

families.name: formal fallback
families.rule: Name the specific invalid form if it has one; formal fallacy only if not. Do not also tag non sequitur for the same step.

families.name: misrepresentation
families.rule: Use one: a distorted restatement that is then attacked (straw man); a clipped quote (out of context); invented words or source (false attribution); an explanation read as an excuse (confusing explanation with excuse).

families.name: others' conduct
families.rule: Use one: a claim or criticism dismissed because the critic does the same (tu quoque); a wrong act defended because others do it (two wrongs).

families.name: accident: ancient and modern
families.rule: Aristotle's sense is about attributes that merely coincide; the modern sense is a rule applied to an exception. Use the one that matches.

families.name: non-cause: ancient and modern
families.rule: Aristotle's sense is a superfluous premise blamed in a reduction to absurdity; for real-world causal claims use false cause.

families.name: selective evidence
families.rule: Contrary evidence absent from the text: suppressed evidence. Contrary evidence stated (or plainly known) but ignored: cherry-picking. A pattern or cluster found by searching and treated as if predicted: Texas sharpshooter. The filter was success or survival: survivorship bias. 'Something improbable happened, so it was designed or rigged': lottery fallacy.

redirects.name: Ambiguous middle term
redirects.note: The middle term shifts meaning; also an instance of equivocation.

redirects.name: Illicit process
redirects.note: General name for illicit major and illicit minor; see also Illicit minor.

redirects.name: Slanting
redirects.note: Name the specific move instead where possible (suppressed evidence, quoting out of context, straw man).

redirects.name: Smear tactic
redirects.note: IEP: a smear of the person is an ad hominem; a smear of the position is a straw man (see Straw man).

entries.name: Accent
entries.definition: Changing the meaning of a sentence by stressing a word or syllable differently (in speech or by emphasis in writing), and then reasoning from the shifted meaning.
entries.example: 'We should not speak ILL of our friends', so it's fine to speak ill of strangers.
required_conditions: A sentence's meaning changes depending on which word or syllable is stressed or emphasised.
The argument relies on the shifted meaning.
The original speaker did not mean it that way.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Emphasis that reflects what the speaker meant.
A quote clipped so that it changes meaning is quoting out of context, not this.

entries.name: Accident
aliases: a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid
entries.definition: Applying a general rule to a case that is a genuine exception, where the circumstances that make the rule sensible are absent.
entries.example: Cutting people with knives is a crime. Surgeons cut people with knives. So surgeons are criminals.
required_conditions: A general rule is applied to a specific case.
The case has a feature that makes the rule's purpose or rationale not apply (state it).
The conclusion relies on applying the rule anyway.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The case is an ordinary instance of the rule.
Applying a rule strictly for a stated reason (fairness, predictability) after considering the exception.

entries.name: Accident (Aristotle's sense)
entries.definition: Aristotle's fallacy of assuming that whatever is true of a thing is also true of something that merely happens to coincide with it (an 'accident'), as if the two were interchangeable. This is different from the modern fallacy of accident (applying a rule to an exception).
entries.example: Coriscus is different from Socrates. Socrates is a man. So Coriscus is different from a man.
required_conditions: Something is true of a thing.
It is concluded to be true of something that merely coincides with it (an incidental attribute or description).
The two are treated as interchangeable.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The two descriptions really are interchangeable for the property in question.
For a general rule misapplied to an exception (the modern sense), use accident.

entries.name: Ad hoc rescue
entries.definition: Saving a cherished claim from contrary evidence by inventing an explanation that has no support except that it saves the claim.
entries.example: The psychic failed because the sceptics' negative energy blocked her powers.
required_conditions: A claim faces counterevidence.
An extra assumption is added to explain the evidence away.
No independent reason for the assumption is given or evident, and it is offered as settling the conflict.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The rescuing assumption has good independent support.

entries.name: Ad hominem (abusive)
entries.definition: Rejecting a claim or argument by attacking the person who made it rather than the reasons they gave.
entries.example: Why listen to his tax plan? He's been divorced three times.
required_conditions: Someone has made a claim or argument.
The reply attacks the person (character, traits, background) rather than the reasons given.
The attack is offered as a reason to reject the claim or argument (stated, or clearly insinuated by sarcasm or 'consider the source'), and the reasons themselves are left unanswered.
The attacked trait is irrelevant to whether the argument's reasons are good. (Expertise or experience can bear on testimony, not on whether stated reasons support the conclusion.)

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Questioning a witness's reliability when the claim rests on their testimony, or relevant character when the question is about the person (for example, fitness for a leadership role).

entries.name: Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise
entries.definition: A syllogism with at least one negative premise but an affirmative conclusion.
entries.example: No reptiles are warm-blooded. All snakes are reptiles. So all snakes are warm-blooded.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism.
At least one premise is negative.
The conclusion is affirmative.

entries.name: Affirming a disjunct
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'P or Q' and 'P' to 'not Q', as if 'or' always meant 'one but not both'.
entries.example: She's either talented or hardworking. She's talented, so she isn't hardworking.
required_conditions: An 'either P or Q' premise is used.
One option is affirmed.
The other option is concluded to be false.
Nothing in the context makes the options mutually exclusive.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The options really exclude each other (on/off, alive/dead), so the 'or' is exclusive.

entries.name: Affirming the consequent
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'If P then Q' and 'Q' to 'P'. Q could be true for some other reason.
entries.example: If the pipes burst, the floor is wet. The floor is wet. So the pipes burst.
required_conditions: A conditional 'if P then Q' is used as a premise.
Q is asserted as true.
P is concluded as definitely following.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Inference to the best explanation: Q is offered as evidence for P after other explanations are considered, and the conclusion is stated as probable.
The conditional is actually a biconditional ('only if' or 'if and only if') in context.

entries.name: Amphiboly
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from a sentence whose grammar allows two readings, relying on the reading that wasn't meant.
entries.example: 'She said on Monday she would sign the contract', so she has to sign it on Monday (when 'on Monday' may say when she spoke, not when she would sign).
required_conditions: A sentence has two readings because of its grammar (not because of one ambiguous word).
The argument relies on one reading.
The speaker meant, or the context supports, the other reading.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Only one reading is plausible in context.
If a single word carries the ambiguity, use equivocation.

entries.name: Anecdotal evidence
entries.definition: Relying on a personal story or a few vivid cases instead of more representative evidence.
entries.example: My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking isn't that harmful.
required_conditions: A conclusion about a general pattern is drawn.
The evidence offered is one or a few personal stories, or unsystematic personal impressions.
Better systematic evidence exists or would be needed for the conclusion.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An anecdote used to illustrate a pattern established on other grounds, or to show that something is possible.
Long, systematically recorded professional observation (for example, a clinic's own logged case series) is not mere anecdote.

entries.name: Anthropomorphism
entries.definition: Projecting human qualities such as intentions or feelings onto something that isn't human and reasoning from that projection.
entries.example: My car hates the cold. It's trying to make me late.
required_conditions: Human mental states or motives are attributed to an animal, object or force.
The thing could not have them (or there is no evidence it does).
A conclusion relies on the attribution.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Attributing feelings an animal can actually have, such as a dog being happy to see you.

entries.name: Appeal to accomplishment
entries.definition: Judging a claim true or false by the achievements of the person making it rather than by the evidence.
entries.example: She founded three companies, so her views on vaccines must be right.
required_conditions: A claim is supported (or attacked) by pointing to the speaker's achievements.
The achievements are in a different field from the claim.
The achievement is treated as settling the matter or as the main reason to accept the claim.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Achievements in the field the claim is about are ordinary evidence of expertise.
The claim concerns a method (statistics, measurement, mathematics) that the person's own field uses.

entries.name: Appeal to authority (illegitimate)
entries.definition: Accepting a claim because someone said it when that person is not a genuine expert on the question, the experts disagree, or the authority is being treated as settling the matter regardless of the evidence.
entries.example: A famous physicist says this diet cures cancer, so it does.
required_conditions: A claim is supported by what some person or body says.
At least one of: the source is not an expert on this question; experts substantially disagree; the source cannot be trusted to be truthful; or the source is misquoted.
The authority is treated as settling the matter.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Relying on a genuine expert speaking within their field, where experts broadly agree; most reasoning from authority is of this kind.

entries.name: Appeal to celebrity
entries.definition: A form of illegitimate appeal to authority: treating a celebrity's endorsement as a reason to accept a product, candidate or claim.
entries.example: A famous actor uses this supplement, so it must work.
required_conditions: A celebrity's endorsement or opinion is cited.
The celebrity is not an expert on the matter.
The endorsement is offered as a reason to accept the product, candidate or claim.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The celebrity speaks within their own field of expertise.

entries.name: Appeal to consequences
entries.definition: Arguing that a factual claim is true or false because believing it would have good or bad results.
entries.example: If there's no afterlife, life is meaningless, so there must be an afterlife.
required_conditions: A factual claim is at issue.
The good or bad consequences of believing it, or of its being true, are cited.
They are offered as a reason the claim is true or false.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Consequences are relevant when deciding what to do rather than what is true.

entries.name: Appeal to emotion
entries.definition: Trying to win acceptance of a claim by stirring up feelings that are not relevant to whether it is true.
entries.example: Think of the children! Vote yes on this measure.
required_conditions: The argument tries to arouse an emotion in the audience.
The emotion is offered as a key reason to accept the conclusion, or to set aside relevant information.
The emotion is not tied to evidence that bears on the conclusion.
No more specific emotion entry (pity, fear, flattery, snobbery, spite, ridicule) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Using emotion while arguing is not wrong; the error is using it as the key premise or to downplay relevant information.

entries.name: Appeal to fear
entries.definition: Trying to win support by stirring up fear rather than giving evidence that the feared outcome is likely.
entries.example: If you don't buy this alarm system, your family could be next.
required_conditions: Fear of an outcome is aroused.
The fear is offered as a reason to accept a claim or course of action.
The feared outcome is unlikely, exaggerated, or unconnected to the action, and is not a well-known risk (well-known risks count as evidenced).

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Warning about a real, well-evidenced danger.
A warning about a risk that is common knowledge, even if no evidence is stated (for example, drink-driving).

entries.name: Appeal to force
entries.definition: Using a threat, open or veiled, to get someone to accept a claim, as if the threat were a reason for believing it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A threat may give a practical reason to act, but not a relevant reason to believe the claim.

entries.name: Appeal to nature
entries.definition: Arguing that something is good because it is 'natural', or bad because it is 'unnatural'.
entries.example: This herbal remedy is natural, so it's safe.
required_conditions: Something is called natural or unnatural, or equivalent wording is used (evolved, ancestral, 'what our bodies are built for').
That label is offered as the reason it is good, safe or right (or bad).
The feature that 'natural' stands for is not spelled out and separately shown to matter.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: 'Natural' stands for a specific property (no additives, long track record) that is separately shown to matter.
Evolutionary history offered as evidence of physiological fit, for a conclusion about fit.
If the conclusion is a moral one drawn from facts, use is-ought.

entries.name: Appeal to novelty
entries.definition: Arguing that something is better or correct simply because it is new.
entries.example: This app was released last week, so it must be better than the old one.
required_conditions: Something is said to be better or correct.
The only reason given is that it is new.

entries.name: Appeal to pity
entries.definition: Using sympathy for someone's situation as a reason to accept a conclusion that their situation doesn't support.
entries.example: I deserve an A; I've had a really hard semester.
required_conditions: Sympathy for someone's situation is aroused.
It is offered as a reason to accept a conclusion.
The situation is irrelevant to that conclusion.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Hardship can be relevant to questions of mercy, need or the fairness of a penalty.

entries.name: Appeal to poverty
entries.definition: Assuming a claim is more likely true, or a person more virtuous, because they are poor.
entries.example: The monk owns nothing, so his views on economics must be wise.
required_conditions: A person's poverty (or a thing's cheapness) is cited.
It is offered as the reason their view is more likely true or the thing better, in a respect unrelated to money.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Cheapness as one indicator of value where there is reason to think it tracks value.

entries.name: Appeal to probability
entries.definition: Treating something that merely could happen as if it will happen, or something that is likely as if it were certain.
entries.example: Someone could hack this account, so someone will.
required_conditions: Something is said to be possible, or likely.
It is then treated as certain or as sure to happen.
The conclusion depends on that upgrade.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Acting with caution on a well-founded probability ('it could happen, so let's insure').

entries.name: Appeal to ridicule
entries.definition: Presenting an opponent's view as laughable in order to dismiss it, without showing what is wrong with it.
entries.example: Remote work? Sure, and let's hold board meetings in our pyjamas. Ha!
required_conditions: An opposing view is mocked or presented as laughable.
The mockery is offered in place of showing what is wrong with the view.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Showing that the view leads to an absurd result (reduction to absurdity) is a legitimate argument.
If the view is simply declared absurd with no mockery, use appeal to the stone.

entries.name: Appeal to snobbery
entries.definition: Urging acceptance of a claim or product by suggesting that discerning, superior people accept it.
entries.example: Only true connoisseurs appreciate this, and you're a connoisseur, aren't you?
required_conditions: A claim or product is associated with a superior or discerning group.
The audience's wish to belong to that group is offered as the reason to accept it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Pointing out that people with relevant expertise choose it, with their reasons.

entries.name: Appeal to spite
entries.definition: Using bitterness or resentment toward a person or group as a reason to accept a claim.
entries.example: Those rich executives never paid their fair share; vote against anything they support.
required_conditions: Resentment toward a person or group is aroused.
The resentment is offered as a reason to accept or reject a claim.
The resentment is not tied to evidence bearing on the claim or decision.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Past wrongdoing cited as evidence about what the person will do (a record of fraud, when deciding whether to hire).

entries.name: Appeal to the people
entries.definition: Arguing that a claim is true, or a practice right, simply because many or most people believe or do it.
entries.example: Millions of people use this remedy, so it must work.
required_conditions: A claim is supported by the fact that many or most people believe or do it.
Popularity is treated as strong or decisive evidence of truth or rightness.
The claim is not itself about what people believe or prefer.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Agreement among people who have studied the question, offered as evidence.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The question is about conventions, tastes or what is popular.
Popular belief is some evidence that a claim is true; the fallacy is overestimating how much.

entries.name: Argument from fallacy
entries.definition: Inferring that a claim is false because an argument offered for it is fallacious or weak. (The Fallacy Files treats this as a case of the broader 'bad reasons fallacy'.)
entries.example: Your argument for vaccination was a slippery slope, so vaccines must not work.
required_conditions: An argument for a claim is shown or alleged to be fallacious or weak.
The claim itself is concluded to be false on that basis.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Concluding only that this argument fails to support the claim.

entries.name: Argument from ignorance
entries.definition: Treating a lack of disproof as proof, or a lack of proof as disproof.
entries.example: No one has proved that ghosts don't exist, so they do.
required_conditions: A claim has not been proven false (or true).
It is concluded to be true (or false) on that basis.
Nothing in the context shows a thorough search was made where evidence would be expected if the claim were true.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A thorough search was done and a proof would have been found if it existed.

entries.name: Argument from incredulity
entries.definition: Concluding that something is false (or must have an extraordinary cause) because you find it hard to believe or imagine.
entries.example: I can't imagine how an eye could evolve, so it couldn't have.
required_conditions: The speaker says they cannot imagine or believe how something could be so.
It is concluded that it is false.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Disbelief backed by a specific reason why the claim is implausible.

entries.name: Argument from repetition
entries.definition: Repeating a claim or argument until people stop disputing it, then citing that lack of objection (or the sheer number of repetitions) as evidence that it is true.
entries.example: I've raised this at every meeting for a year and nobody argues with it any more, so it's obviously right.
required_conditions: A claim is restated many times, in one exchange or over time.
Others' having stopped objecting, or the number of repetitions, is cited as evidence that the claim is true (for example, 'nobody disputes this any more').
No new support is given.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Restating a point that was not addressed, while asking for a response.
Exasperated restating in reply to a counterargument ('I've told you three times: it works'), without citing the repetition or others' silence as evidence, is proof by assertion, not this.

entries.name: Argument from silence
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from the absence of a statement or record, when that absence has other likely explanations.
entries.example: His diary never mentions his brother, so he didn't have one.
required_conditions: A source does not mention something.
It is concluded that the thing did not happen or the author did not know of it.
There is no strong reason to expect the source would have mentioned it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The source would very likely have mentioned it if it were so.

entries.name: Availability heuristic (as a fallacy)
entries.definition: Judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, and deciding on that basis.
entries.example: I'll drive instead of flying; you always hear about plane crashes.
required_conditions: A judgement about how common or likely something is is made.
The judgement rests on how easily memorable examples come to mind.
Actual frequency data are available and point the other way.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Recall of cases that really are typical. If the text cites a vivid case as its reason, use misleading vividness instead.

entries.name: Avoiding the issue
entries.definition: Going off on a tangent instead of addressing the issue one is supposed to address.
entries.example: Asked about the budget overrun, the minister talks about the great new stadium.
required_conditions: An issue is under discussion.
The arguer addresses something else.
The original issue is left unresolved.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Settling a prior issue first, when the original issue really depends on it.

entries.name: Baconian fallacy
entries.definition: Supposing that historians can reach the whole truth simply by piling up individual pieces of evidence, without questions or theories to guide them.
entries.example: Collect every document from the period and the meaning of the war will become obvious.
required_conditions: It is claimed that historical truth can be reached simply by gathering facts.
The role of questions and interpretation is denied.

entries.name: Bandwagon
aliases: argumentum ad novitatem (as IEP uses the term)
entries.definition: Arguing that a claim is correct because more and more people are coming to believe it.
entries.example: Everyone's switching to this phone, so it must be the best.
required_conditions: A claim is supported by the fact that more and more people are adopting it.
The trend is treated as a reason it is true or right.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Pointing out that what most people believe after consideration is likely true, all things considered, is not fallacious.

entries.name: Base-rate fallacy
entries.definition: Judging a probability from specific evidence (such as a test result) while ignoring how common the thing is to begin with.
entries.example: The test is 99% accurate and I tested positive, so I almost certainly have this disease that affects 1 in 100,000 people.
required_conditions: A probability about a specific case is estimated from specific evidence such as a test result or description.
The base rate (how common the thing is overall) is relevant and is known or knowable.
The estimate ignores or badly underweights that base rate.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The base rate is unknown and the speaker says so.
The specific evidence is so strong that the base rate makes little difference, and this is shown.
If 'the chance of this evidence if innocent' is presented as the chance of innocence, use prosecutor's fallacy.

entries.name: Begging the question
entries.definition: Supporting a conclusion with a premise that is only acceptable to someone who already accepts the conclusion, so the argument gives no independent reason. Includes arguing in a circle, where the conclusion reappears, openly or reworded, among the premises.
entries.example: Her advice is trustworthy because she's an honest person, and she's honest because her advice is trustworthy.
required_conditions: A conclusion is argued for.
A premise asserts the conclusion, or something the audience could only accept if they already accepted the conclusion.
The premise is not independently supported.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A premise that can be defended independently of the conclusion is reasonable to use.

entries.name: Bulverism
entries.definition: Assuming a view is wrong and then explaining why the other person holds it (their bias, psychology or upbringing) instead of showing that it is wrong.
entries.example: You only think the economy is doing badly because you're a pessimist.
required_conditions: A view is assumed to be wrong without showing it.
The reply explains the view by the holder's psychology, bias or upbringing.
The explanation is offered in place of showing that the view is wrong.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Explaining why someone holds a view after the view has been shown to be wrong on independent grounds.

entries.name: Cherry-picking
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from a selected part of the evidence while the rest of it, which is stated or plainly known, points the other way or weakens it and goes unanswered. Unlike suppressed evidence, the contrary evidence is in plain view.
entries.example: The report shows test scores rose at three of the ten pilot schools and fell at the other seven. The programme clearly works: look at those three schools.
required_conditions: The arguer selects a subset of the available or stated data.
The rest of the data, stated or plainly known, points the other way or dilutes the subset.
The conclusion rests on the subset, and the rest gets no answer.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The subset is singled out for a stated, independent reason (for example, a subgroup named before the data came in).
Highlighting the strongest examples while acknowledging and answering the rest.
If the contrary evidence is absent from the text, use suppressed evidence instead.

entries.name: Commutation of conditionals
entries.definition: Inferring 'If Q then P' from 'If P then Q'. A conditional does not automatically run in reverse.

Any direct answer would commit the respondent to that claim.

entries.name: Composition
entries.definition: Assuming that what is true of the parts, or of each member, must be true of the whole or the group.
entries.example: Every player on the team is a star, so the team will be great.
required_conditions: A property of the parts or members is established.
The whole or group is concluded to have that property.
No reason is given why this property carries over from parts to whole.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Properties that do carry over, such as weight or being made of a material, often transfer from parts to whole.

entries.name: Confirmation bias (as a fallacy)
entries.definition: Seeking out or giving weight only to evidence that supports what you already believe, and not looking for evidence against it.
entries.example: I only read reviews that agree with me, and they all prove I'm right.
required_conditions: A conclusion is supported by evidence.
The evidence cited is selected only for agreeing with the conclusion.
Relevant contrary evidence was available and ignored, because of a prior belief.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Citing supporting evidence while dealing with the contrary evidence.
If the text omits known contrary evidence, consider suppressed evidence (a text-level question).

entries.name: Confusing an explanation with an excuse
entries.definition: Treating an account of why something happened as if it were a justification of it, or rejecting the explanation because it seems to excuse.
entries.example: You say poverty contributes to crime? So you think criminals aren't responsible?
required_conditions: Someone explains why something happened.
The reply treats the explanation as a justification or excuse, or rejects it because it seems to excuse.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The speaker does in fact offer the explanation as an excuse.

entries.name: Confusing necessary and sufficient conditions
entries.definition: Treating a condition that must be present for something to happen as if it were enough by itself to make it happen, or the reverse.
entries.example: Oxygen is needed for fire. There is oxygen in this room, so there will be a fire.
required_conditions: A condition is established as necessary (required) for an outcome, or as sufficient (enough) for it.
The argument treats it as the other kind of condition.
The conclusion depends on that switch.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The condition is in fact both necessary and sufficient, and this is shown.

entries.name: Conjunction fallacy
entries.definition: Judging that two things together are more likely than one of them alone. A combination can never be more probable than either part.
entries.example: Dana studied environmental science and organises beach clean-ups. Which is more likely: (a) Dana works at a bank, or (b) Dana works at a bank and volunteers for a conservation group? Choosing (b) is the fallacy.
required_conditions: Two outcomes are compared: one single outcome and that outcome combined with another.
The combination is judged more probable than the single outcome.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Judging that a detail makes a story more plausible as an explanation, without claiming it is more probable.

entries.name: Converse accident
entries.definition: Generalizing from exceptional cases to a rule meant for ordinary cases.
entries.example: Patients in pain are allowed morphine, so everyone should be allowed morphine.
required_conditions: Atypical or exceptional cases are cited.
A general rule or claim for ordinary cases is drawn from them.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Deliberately setting a rule that covers the exceptions as a separate category.
Do not also tag hasty generalization for the same step.

entries.name: Courtier's reply
entries.definition: Dismissing a criticism by claiming the critic hasn't studied the subject in enough depth to comment, without answering the criticism.
entries.example: You can't criticise astrology until you've read the major astrological texts.
required_conditions: A criticism is raised.
The reply says the critic lacks the knowledge or training to comment.

The criticism itself is not answered, and either it does not depend on the specialised knowledge, or the reply denies the critic standing to criticise at all, regardless of content, without naming any misunderstanding.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The criticism actually rests on a misunderstanding that the specialised knowledge would correct, and the reply says what it is.

entries.name: Cum hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: with this, therefore because of this
entries.definition: Concluding that because two things occur together, one causes the other.
entries.example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, so ice cream causes drowning.
required_conditions: Two things are shown to occur together (a correlation).
One is concluded to cause the other.
At least one plausible alternative (chance, a third factor, the reverse direction) is left open, and the causal claim is stated as established rather than as a hypothesis to test.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Correlations are often good evidence of causation when alternatives are addressed.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A correlation can support a causal conclusion once coincidence, a confounding cause and the reverse direction have been ruled out.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A correlation plus a comparison group or a known mechanism, offered as grounds to investigate.
If the argument does address causes but misses an obvious third factor, use ignoring a common cause.

entries.name: Overfitting (curve fitting)
entries.definition: Fitting a model so closely to existing data, noise included, that it describes the past well but predicts poorly, and then trusting its predictions. Fitting a curve to data is not itself a fallacy.
entries.example: Our 30-variable formula explains every past election perfectly, so it will predict the next one.
required_conditions: A model is fitted to existing data with many adjustable parts.
It fits past data closely but has not been tested on new data.
Its predictions are presented as reliable because of the close fit.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Fitting a curve to data is a normal process; the error is fitting it so closely that it tracks noise.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The model has been checked on data it was not fitted to.

entries.name: Dangling comparative
entries.definition: Using a comparative word like 'better' or 'more' without saying what is being compared to, so the claim sounds meaningful but can't be checked.
entries.example: Our toothpaste cleans 50% better!
required_conditions: A comparative ('better', 'more', 'less') is used.
What it is compared with is not stated or recoverable from context.
The claim is offered as informative.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The comparison class is clear from context.

entries.name: Definitional retreat
entries.definition: Changing the meaning of a key word once an objection is raised, so the claim survives in name only.
entries.example: When I said the plan 'worked', I meant it started a conversation.
required_conditions: A claim is made using a word in its ordinary sense.
After an objection, the word is given a different or narrower meaning.
The claim is then presented as having survived the objection.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Openly clarifying what was meant from the start, when the original wording was ambiguous.
Openly conceding that the original claim was too strong.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

entries.name: Denying a conjunct
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'not both P and Q' and 'not P' to 'Q'. Both could be false.
entries.example: You can't be both at the office and at the gym. You're not at the office, so you must be at the gym.
required_conditions: A premise says 'not both P and Q'.
One of them is denied.
The other is concluded to be true.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The context establishes that exactly one of the two must hold.

entries.name: Denying the antecedent
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'If P then Q' and 'not P' to 'not Q'. Q could still be true for some other reason.
entries.example: If it rains, the game is cancelled. It didn't rain. So the game wasn't cancelled.
required_conditions: A conditional 'if P then Q' is used as a premise.
P is denied.
Not-Q is concluded as following.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The speaker means 'only if P then Q' (P is required for Q), which makes the inference valid.

entries.name: Disregarding known science
entries.definition: Making a claim that ignores or contradicts well-established science without addressing it.
entries.example: This engine runs forever on a single tank of water.
required_conditions: A claim is made.
It conflicts with well-established scientific findings (identify them).
The conflict is not addressed.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Challenging a finding with new evidence, and saying so.
A claim that engages the established evidence and argues against it is dissent, not this.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Disregarding Known Science"

entries.name: Division
entries.definition: Assuming that what is true of a whole or group must be true of each of its parts or members.
entries.example: The university is world-famous, so every professor there is world-famous.
required_conditions: A property of a whole or group is established.
Each part or member is concluded to have that property.
No reason is given why this property carries over from whole to parts.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Properties that do carry down to every member (being made of steel, belonging to the group by definition).

entries.name: Division of words (Aristotle)
entries.definition: Aristotle's fallacy of splitting apart words that should be read together, which changes the meaning, as in '5 is 2 and 3, so 5 is even and odd'.
entries.example: Five is two and three; two is even and three is odd; so five is both even and odd.
required_conditions: Words that should be read together are split apart (or a statement true in a combined sense is read in a divided sense).
The changed meaning is used to reach the conclusion.

entries.name: Doorman fallacy
entries.definition: Reducing a role to its most visible task and judging its value or cost on that basis, missing the less visible value it provides.
entries.example: A doorman just opens doors, so replace him with an automatic door.
required_conditions: A role or service is judged by its most visible task.
It has other, less visible functions or value.
The conclusion (for example, to replace it) relies on overlooking them.

entries.name: Double counting
entries.definition: Counting the same outcome or piece of evidence more than once, so probabilities or totals come out too high.
entries.example: A survey says 60% of residents use the bus and 50% use the train, so 110% of residents use public transport (people who use both were counted twice).
required_conditions: Outcomes or items are added up.
Some are counted in more than one category.
The total is presented as a meaningful sum (often exceeding 100%).

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Categories are explicitly overlapping and the total is not presented as a sum.

entries.name: Double standard
entries.definition: Judging two relevantly similar people or cases by different standards.
entries.example: When our candidate changes his mind it's growth; when theirs does it's flip-flopping.
required_conditions: Two cases are judged by different standards.
The same standard should apply because they are alike in the relevant respects.
The conclusion relies on the difference.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The cases differ in a relevant way, so different standards are justified.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Double Standard"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: If the speaker exempts their own case from a rule, use special pleading instead.
Asking that a stated test be applied consistently is legitimate, unless it is used to dismiss the original criticism.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Double Standard"

entries.name: Ecological fallacy
entries.definition: Drawing conclusions about individuals from statistics about the groups they belong to.
entries.example: Richer states vote for party X, so richer people vote for party X.
required_conditions: Data are about groups (regions, populations).
A conclusion is drawn about individuals within them.
The group-level pattern is taken to establish the same pattern for individuals (or a particular person) without individual-level data.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Group data are used only as a clue, with individual-level data to confirm.
Group figures do not prove an individual-level link, but they don't disprove one either.

entries.name: I'm entitled to my opinion
entries.definition: Treating the right to hold an opinion as if it were a reason the opinion is correct or exempt from criticism.
entries.example: You can show me all the data you want; I'm entitled to my opinion.
required_conditions: A view is criticised or evidence against it is offered.
The reply is that one has a right to one's opinion.
The right is treated as answering the criticism.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Asserting the right to hold a view as a point about freedom, without claiming it answers the evidence.

sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "I'm entitled to my opinion"

entries.name: Equivocation
entries.definition: Using a word or phrase in one sense in one part of an argument and in a different sense in another, so the argument only seems to work.
entries.example: A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark.
required_conditions: A word or phrase occurs more than once in the argument.
It has one meaning in one place and a different meaning in another (state both).
The conclusion follows only if the meanings are treated as the same.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The word keeps one meaning throughout (substitute a definition at each use to check).
Puns or wordplay not offered as argument.
When the shifting word is the middle term of a categorical syllogism, report it as equivocation and add '(four terms)'.

entries.name: Etymological fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that a word's original or historical meaning is its real or current meaning.
entries.example: 'Decimate' originally meant killing one in ten, so you're wrong to use it for heavy losses.
required_conditions: A word's origin or earlier meaning is cited.
It is offered as the word's real or present meaning.
Current usage differs and the argument relies on the old meaning.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Using etymology to explain how a meaning arose, not to set the present meaning.

entries.name: Exaggeration
entries.definition: Overstating a key step in an argument so that the conclusion looks better supported than it is.
entries.example: Everyone knows the new rule has been a total disaster, so it must be repealed.
required_conditions: A claim that is a crucial step in the reasoning is overstated.
The argument relies on the overstated version.
The overstatement is meant literally.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Jokes and figures of speech not meant literally.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Exaggeration"

entries.name: Exclusive premises
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion from a syllogism whose premises are both negative. Two denials do not connect the terms.
entries.example: No fish are mammals. No birds are fish. So no birds are mammals.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism.
Both premises are negative.
A conclusion is drawn.

entries.name: Existential fallacy
entries.definition: Drawing a conclusion that says something exists from premises that are only universal ('all' or 'no') and so don't guarantee that anything exists.
entries.example: All trespassers will be fined. So some trespassers will be fined.
required_conditions: All premises are universal ('all' or 'no').
The conclusion asserts that something exists ('some ...').
Nothing in the context establishes that the class has members.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The context makes it clear the class is non-empty (for example, it is about people in the room).

entries.name: Fake precision
entries.definition: Presenting a figure as more exact than the evidence can support, which gives it unearned authority.
entries.example: This policy will save exactly 1,483,227 jobs.
required_conditions: A figure is given with more precision than its source or method can support.
The precision is used to make the claim seem more authoritative or the comparison more decisive.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Precise figures from exact counts, or estimates reported with their margin of error.

entries.name: Fallacy of exhaustive effort
entries.definition: Assuming that when some conditions for the best outcome can't be met, meeting as many of the rest as possible must give the next-best outcome.
entries.example: We can't have the ideal team of five, so hiring four of the five ideal people must be the next-best option (although the fifth role was what tied them together).
required_conditions: Some conditions for an ideal outcome cannot be met.
It is concluded that meeting as many of the others as possible gives the next best outcome.

entries.name: Fallacy of the sheep
entries.definition: Comparing raw counts between groups of very different sizes instead of comparing rates.
entries.example: There were ten cases among right-handers and only one among left-handers, so left-handed people are safer.
required_conditions: Raw counts are compared between groups.
The groups differ greatly in size.
A conclusion about rates or risk is drawn from the counts.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The groups are of similar size, or the comparison is about totals, not rates.

entries.name: False analogy
entries.definition: Arguing that because two things are alike in some ways they are alike in another way, when the similarities are not relevant to that point or the differences matter more.
entries.example: Employees are like nails: they work best when you hit them on the head.
required_conditions: Two things are compared.
A conclusion about one is drawn from the other.
They differ in a respect relevant to the conclusion (state it).

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An analogy where the shared features are the ones that matter to the conclusion.
An analogy used to illustrate, not to argue.

entries.name: False attribution
entries.definition: Supporting a point with words a person never said, or with a source that does not exist.
entries.example: As Einstein said, 'Compound interest is the most powerful force in the universe.'
required_conditions: A claim is supported by attributing words or findings to a source.
The source did not say it, does not exist, or is misrepresented (this must be checked against the source).
The argument relies on the attribution.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Honest paraphrase that fairly captures the source.
A real source that is not qualified on the topic is appeal to authority; a real quote that is clipped is quoting out of context.

entries.name: False balance
entries.definition: Presenting two positions as equally supported, for example in news coverage, when the evidence strongly favours one of them.
entries.example: Giving equal airtime to one climate scientist and one sceptic, as if expert opinion were evenly split.
required_conditions: Two positions are presented as equally credible.
The evidence strongly favours one of them.
The presentation implies they are on a par.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Presenting views as equally weighted when the evidence is genuinely mixed.

entries.name: False cause
entries.definition: Concluding that one thing causes another when the only support is that they occur together or in sequence, or when an obvious alternative explanation (a common cause, reversed direction, or chance) has not been ruled out.
entries.example: Countries with more Nobel laureates eat more chocolate, so chocolate makes people smarter.
required_conditions: A causal conclusion is drawn.
The only support is that the two occur together or in sequence, or an obvious alternative (a common cause, the reverse direction, chance) is left open.
No more specific causal entry (post hoc, correlation, common cause, reverse causation, single cause, regression) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A tentative causal hypothesis offered for testing.

entries.name: False dilemma
entries.definition: Presenting too few options, often just two, as the only ones, when others exist.
entries.example: Either we cut the school's art programme or we go bankrupt.
required_conditions: A choice is presented between options as though they were the only ones.
At least one further reasonable option exists (name it).
The conclusion relies on eliminating the stated options.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The options really are exhaustive (a true dichotomy), or the speaker names the main options without claiming they are the only ones.

entries.name: False equivalence
entries.definition: Implying that two things, often two sides' cases, are roughly equal in strength or seriousness when one is much weaker or much less serious, glossing over the difference.
entries.example: Both of them told lies, so the man who misstated his age is as dishonest as the man who committed fraud.
required_conditions: Two things are presented as equivalent.
They share some feature, but differ greatly in a relevant respect (state it).
The conclusion relies on treating them as equal.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Comparing things in the respect in which they really are alike.

entries.name: Far-fetched hypothesis
entries.definition: Offering a bizarre explanation as the correct one without first ruling out simpler, more likely explanations.
entries.example: The crop circles must have been made by aliens.
required_conditions: An explanation is offered for something.
It is improbable (bizarre or extraordinary).
Simpler, more likely explanations have not been ruled out.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An unusual explanation offered after likelier ones have been ruled out.
Suggesting an unusual explanation as something to test.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Far-Fetched Hypothesis"

entries.name: Feedback fallacy
entries.definition: Trusting an evaluation as objective, and acting on it, without checking whether its source is disinterested.
entries.example: My manager says I'm the problem, so I must be (the manager is defending his own decisions).
required_conditions: An evaluation (feedback, a review) is relied on.
Its source has an interest or bias that is not checked.
It is treated as objective.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A reviewer's stake is a reason to check the evaluation, not proof that it is wrong.

entries.name: Form of expression (Aristotle)
entries.definition: Being misled by the grammatical form of a word into treating it as belonging to the wrong category, for example treating a word that sounds like an action as if it named an action.
entries.example: 'Flourishing' ends in -ing like 'running', so flourishing must be something a person does.
required_conditions: A word's grammatical form suggests a category (an action, a quality, a gender) it does not belong to.
The argument relies on treating it as belonging to that category.

entries.name: Formal fallacy
entries.definition: The general name for any argument whose form is invalid, so that true premises could still yield a false conclusion. Most invalid forms have no special name; when this label is used, show a counterexample with the same form.
entries.example: Some doctors are runners. Some runners are teenagers. So some doctors are teenagers.
required_conditions: The argument is offered as deductive: the conclusion is presented as following necessarily.
An argument with exactly the same form can be given that has true premises and a false conclusion (show it).
No more specific formal entry describes the invalid step.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A strong inductive or explanatory argument that is not deductively valid; judge it by inductive standards, not as a formal fallacy.
An argument that is valid once an obvious, stated-elsewhere premise is supplied.
Do not also tag non sequitur for the same step.

entries.name: Four terms
entries.definition: A syllogism that uses four distinct terms instead of three, often because one word is used in two senses, so the premises never actually connect.
entries.example: Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A sandwich is better than nothing. So a sandwich is better than eternal happiness.
required_conditions: The argument is presented as a syllogism linking two terms through a third.
One apparent term is used in two different senses, or two different terms are treated as one, so there are four terms.
The conclusion depends on the link that the shift creates.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The repeated word has the same meaning in both premises (check by substituting a definition).
Report it as equivocation with '(four terms)' added; this entry gives the syllogism analysis.

A run of one outcome is cited.

entries.definition: Judging a claim or practice good or bad by where it came from rather than by its present merits.

entries.name: Goomba fallacy
entries.definition: Pinning views expressed by different people in a crowd onto the crowd as a whole, then calling the group inconsistent.
entries.example: Critics say the film is too long and also say it's too rushed. Make up your minds!

entries.name: Group think
entries.definition: Substituting loyalty to or pride in one's group for reasons, so that the group's view is accepted without examination.

required_conditions: A group's view or policy is accepted.

entries.name: Guilt by association
entries.definition: Judging a claim or person by the company they keep or the groups they're linked to, rather than on the merits.

required_conditions: A person or claim is linked to a group, person or idea that the audience dislikes.
The link is offered as a reason to reject the claim or condemn the person.
No evidence is given that the association bears on the specific claim.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The association is real evidence about the specific claim or about a witness's reliability.
Showing that someone actually shares the specific commitment being criticised.

entries.name: Hasty generalization
entries.definition: Drawing a general conclusion from too few cases to support it.
entries.example: My two neighbours from that city were rude, so people from that city are rude.
required_conditions: A general conclusion about a group is drawn.
The evidence is a sample of the group.
The sample is too small, or the conclusion is too sweeping, for the evidence.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A small sample can suffice when the population is known to be uniform in the relevant respect.
A tentative conclusion stated with appropriate caution.
Do not also tag converse accident or secundum quid for the same step.
A small sample with a large, consistent effect, used for a reversible or low-stakes decision.
If the doubt is about how the sample was chosen rather than its size, use unrepresentative sample.

entries.name: Hedging
entries.definition: Quietly qualifying a claim to dodge counterevidence and then acting as if the original, stronger claim still stood.
entries.example: I said the stock would rise, and I meant eventually, in some sense.
required_conditions: A claim is stated.
Faced with counterevidence, it is reworded to something weaker.
The original, stronger claim is then treated as still standing.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Openly accepting counterevidence and admitting the original claim was wrong is not this.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Hedging"

entries.name: Historian's fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that people in the past had the information we have now, and judging their decisions accordingly.
entries.example: The generals should have known the attack was coming; it's obvious from the records we have now.
required_conditions: A past decision is judged.
Information that the decision-makers did not have at the time is assumed to have been available to them.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Judging the decision in light of what the decision-makers knew at the time.

entries.name: Historical fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that a result came about only because a particular process was performed, when the process may have nothing to do with it.
entries.example: Our children turned out well because we followed this parenting book.
required_conditions: A result is attributed to a process that was carried out.
No evidence is given that the process produced the result, and the result could plausibly be present anyway (say why).

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Attribution backed by a before-and-after comparison or a known mechanism.

entries.name: Homunculus fallacy
entries.definition: Explaining something by appeal to a smaller version of the same thing, which leaves the original question unanswered.
entries.example: We see because a little viewer in the brain looks at the images from our eyes.
required_conditions: Something is explained.
The explanation calls on a smaller agent or process with the same ability.
The original question is left unanswered.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A layered explanation in which each layer is simpler than the one above.

entries.name: Hot hand fallacy
entries.definition: Believing that a streak of successes in a chance process makes further successes more likely.
entries.example: I've won five hands in a row, so I'm on a hot streak and should bet more.
required_conditions: The process is one of independent chance (or known to behave like it).
A streak of successes is cited.
Further success is concluded to be more likely because of the streak.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: In skilled activities a streak can reflect real changes in form or conditions; do not flag by default.

entries.name: Ideology-driven argumentation
entries.definition: Treating a contested doctrine of one's own ideology as settled, when the conclusion depends on it and the arguer cannot or will not defend it.
entries.example: Since the free market always produces the best outcome, any regulation is harmful.
required_conditions: A conclusion depends on a contested doctrine.
The doctrine is treated as settled.
No defence of the doctrine is offered when it is challenged.
No more specific entry fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Reasoning from openly stated premises to an audience that shares them.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Ideology-Driven Argumentation"

entries.name: If-by-whiskey
entries.definition: Answering a question by supporting both sides, using emotionally loaded terms so that each side hears agreement.
entries.example: If by 'growth' you mean jobs for families, I'm for it; if you mean concrete over our parks, I'm against it.
required_conditions: A question is asked that calls for a position.
The answer supports both sides, depending on how the issue is described.
Loaded terms are used so each side hears agreement.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A conditional answer that clearly states which specific cases fall on each side.

entries.name: Illicit contraposition
entries.definition: Applying contraposition (swap and negate both terms) to a categorical statement where it is not valid, such as 'No A are B' or 'Some A are B'.
entries.example: No cats are dogs. So no non-dogs are non-cats.
required_conditions: A statement of the form 'No A are B' or 'Some A are B' is accepted.
Its contrapositive ('No non-B are non-A' / 'Some non-B are non-A') is concluded from it alone.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Contraposing 'All A are B' or 'Some A are not B' is valid.

source.title: The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis)
source.locator: entry "Illicit Contraposition"

entries.name: Illicit conversion
entries.definition: Swapping the subject and predicate of a categorical statement where the swap is not valid, such as going from 'All A are B' to 'All B are A'.
entries.example: All surgeons are doctors, so all doctors are surgeons.
required_conditions: A categorical statement 'All A are B' (or 'Some A are not B') is accepted.
'All B are A' (or 'Some B are not A') is concluded from it alone.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Converting 'No A are B' or 'Some A are B' is valid.

source.title: The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis)
source.locator: entry "Illicit Conversion"

entries.name: Illicit major
aliases: illicit process of the major term
entries.definition: A syllogism whose conclusion says something about all of the major term's class when the major premise said something about only part of it.
entries.example: All dogs are mammals. No cats are dogs. So no cats are mammals.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism.
The major term (predicate of the conclusion) refers to all of its class in the conclusion.
It refers only to part of its class in the major premise.

entries.name: Illicit minor
aliases: illicit process of the minor term
entries.definition: A syllogism whose conclusion says something about all of the minor term's class when the minor premise said something about only part of it.
entries.example: All squares are rectangles. All squares are shapes. So all shapes are rectangles.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism.
The minor term (subject of the conclusion) refers to all of its class in the conclusion.
It refers only to part of its class in the minor premise.

entries.name: Improper transposition
entries.definition: Inferring 'If not P then not Q' from 'If P then Q'. The valid move is 'If not Q then not P'.
entries.example: If you study, you'll pass. So if you don't study, you won't pass.
required_conditions: A conditional 'if P then Q' is accepted.
'If not P then not Q' is concluded from it alone.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The valid contrapositive 'if not Q then not P'.
If the speaker also asserts not-P and concludes not-Q, use denying the antecedent instead.

entries.name: Inconsistency
entries.definition: Relying on two or more claims that cannot all be true, as if all of them supported the conclusion, without noticing the conflict.
entries.example: I never generalize, because people who generalize are always hypocrites.
required_conditions: Two or more claims are relied on in the argument.
They cannot all be true together (show the clash).
No more specific entry (kettle logic, special pleading, double standard) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A change of mind that is acknowledged.
Apparent conflicts that disappear on a fair reading (different times, respects or senses).
Deriving a contradiction on purpose, to reject an assumption (reduction to absurdity), is not this.

entries.name: Independence fallacy
entries.definition: Treating events as independent and multiplying their probabilities when they are in fact linked, which can make a combination look far rarer than it is.
entries.example: Each of the plane's two engines fails once in 10,000 flights, so both failing on one flight is a 1-in-100-million event (ignoring that they share fuel and maintenance).
required_conditions: Probabilities of several events are multiplied to get the chance of them all happening.
There is a known or plausible link between the events.
The link is ignored, and the conclusion depends on the resulting low figure.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The events are shown to be independent.

entries.name: Inductive conversion
entries.definition: Reasoning from 'all (or most) A are B' to 'all (or most) B are A'.
entries.example: Most jockeys are short, so most short people are jockeys.
required_conditions: It is accepted that all or most A are B.
It is concluded that all or most B are A.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Inductive Conversion"

entries.name: Inflation of conflict
entries.definition: Arguing that because experts disagree on some point, nothing can be known in that field or the field as a whole is unreliable.
entries.example: Economists argue about interest rates, so economics is just guesswork.
required_conditions: Experts are shown to disagree on some point.
It is concluded that nothing can be known in the field, or that the field is unreliable as a whole.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Concluding that the specific point in dispute is unsettled.

entries.name: Intensional fallacy
entries.definition: Swapping one name or description for another that refers to the same thing inside a context where the wording matters, such as statements about what someone knows, believes, said or wants, or about what is necessary.
entries.example: Lena believes the author of that anonymous novel is brilliant. Unknown to her, the author is her dentist. So Lena believes her dentist is brilliant.
required_conditions: A statement is made about what someone knows, believes, wants or said, or about what is necessary or possible.
A name or description inside it is replaced with another that refers to the same thing.
The replaced statement is concluded to be true.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Substituting co-referring terms in ordinary factual statements ('the masked man is tall', so 'my father is tall') is valid.

entries.name: Intentional fallacy
entries.definition: In literary criticism: treating the author's intention as what settles a work's meaning or value, rather than the work itself. The term is a critic's thesis and is disputed.
entries.example: The author says it's not about war, so the war allegory everyone sees isn't there.
required_conditions: A work's meaning or value is being judged.
The author's intention is treated as settling the matter.
The work itself is not examined.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Using an author's stated intention as one piece of evidence; whether this is fallacious is disputed among critics.
The question really is what the author meant or intended to do.

entries.name: Inverse gambler's fallacy
entries.definition: Concluding from one unlikely outcome that the process behind it must have been repeated many times before.
entries.example: He rolled double sixes on his first throw, so he must have been playing for hours.
required_conditions: A single unlikely outcome is observed.
It is concluded that the process must have been repeated many times before.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: There is independent evidence of earlier repetitions.

entries.name: Ipse dixit
entries.definition: Presenting a contested claim as true without any support, as if it were self-evident. (When the support offered is 'trust me, I'm an expert', use appeal to authority.)
entries.example: It's simply true that this is the best policy. End of story.
required_conditions: A contested claim is asserted.
No support is given.
It is presented as self-evident or beyond question.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Stating common knowledge, or a point both sides already accept.
'Trust me, I'm the expert' is an appeal to authority, not this.

entries.name: Irrelevant conclusion
entries.definition: Offering an argument that may be fine in itself but supports a different conclusion from the one at issue.
entries.example: The defendant can't be guilty of fraud; the fraud caused great suffering and fraud is a terrible crime (which argues that fraud is bad, not that he did it).
required_conditions: An argument is offered on a stated issue.
The argument supports a different conclusion.
That different conclusion is presented as settling the issue.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Evidence relevant to a related question (such as leniency rather than guilt), offered for that question.

entries.name: Is-ought fallacy

required_conditions: The premises state only what is the case.
The conclusion states what ought to be done or what is good.
No ought-premise is stated or obviously implied.

entries.name: Jumping to conclusions
entries.definition: Reaching a conclusion without relevant evidence that was readily available, when there was time and it was practical to get it.
entries.example: The lights are off at her house, so she must have moved away.
required_conditions: A conclusion is drawn.
Relevant evidence was not gathered or considered.
There was time and opportunity to do so.
No more specific entry fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Quick decisions are not always wrong; it is the fallacy only when there was time and the effort was not prohibitive.

entries.name: Kettle logic
entries.definition: Offering several defences that contradict each other, in the hope that one will work.
entries.example: I never borrowed your kettle; it was already broken; and anyway I gave it back undamaged.
required_conditions: Several arguments are offered for one conclusion.
At least two of them contradict each other.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Arguing in the alternative, where it is made explicit that each argument stands on its own ('even if X, still Y').

entries.name: Lack of proportion
entries.definition: Treating a clearly trivial point as decisive, or a clearly decisive point as trivial, so that it gets the wrong weight in reaching the conclusion.
entries.example: One typo in the report means none of its findings can be trusted.
required_conditions: A point is given a weight in the argument.
The weight is clearly out of line with its significance (show it).
No more specific entry (exaggeration, oversimplification, quibbling) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Reasonable people giving different weights to a point.

entries.name: Line-drawing fallacy
entries.definition: Concluding that because no sharp line can be drawn between two things, there is no real difference between them, or that a vague term can't be used.
entries.example: One more grain doesn't make a heap, so there's no such thing as a heap of sand.
required_conditions: A term with borderline cases (vague) is in play.
It is argued that because no exact line can be drawn, there is no real difference or the term is meaningless.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A vague term is not hopelessly vague; borderline cases leave clear cases clear.

entries.name: Loaded label
entries.definition: Using a descriptive label whose connotations assume the point in dispute.
entries.example: This 'death tax' should be repealed.
required_conditions: A label is applied to a person, view or thing.
The label builds in the contested conclusion.
The argument uses the label in place of support for that conclusion.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A label that is not inherently fallacious and is accurate and supported.

entries.name: Loaded language
entries.definition: Using emotionally charged or value-laden words, in what is presented as a neutral argument, to push the listener toward a conclusion.
entries.example: The bureaucrats' job-killing scheme will be voted on today.
required_conditions: Emotionally charged or value-laden words are used.
They appear in what is presented as a neutral or objective description.
They push the audience toward a conclusion for which no reason has been given.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The charged word is accurate and supported by evidence.
Openly evaluative writing (an editorial, a closing argument) that does not claim to be neutral.

entries.name: Logic chopping
entries.definition: Obscuring the issue with needlessly technical distinctions or formal machinery that don't bear on the real question.
entries.example: Before we discuss the budget, define 'spending' in predicate logic.
required_conditions: Technical distinctions or formal detail are introduced.
They do not bear on the question at issue.
They are used to delay or block a conclusion on that question.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A technical distinction that changes the answer.
