entries.name: Lottery fallacy
entries.definition: Treating an outcome as too improbable to be chance because that particular outcome was unlikely, while ignoring that some unlikely outcome was bound to happen.
entries.example: The odds that she in particular would win were 1 in 10 million, so the draw must have been rigged.
required_conditions: A specific outcome is noted to have been very unlikely.
It is concluded that the outcome needs a special explanation (design, rigging).
Some outcome of similar improbability was bound to occur.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The outcome was specified in advance, or matches a pattern that rigging would predict.

entries.name: Ludic fallacy
entries.definition: Applying the clean, known odds of a game or model to a real situation while ignoring a specific, identifiable way the real situation differs.
entries.example: Our model treats market moves like coin flips, so a crash this size is effectively impossible.
required_conditions: Odds from a game, model or textbook case are applied to a real situation.
A specific difference between the real situation and the model is identifiable.
That difference is ignored and the conclusion depends on it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Using a model while stating its limits.
All models leave things out; that alone is not this fallacy.

entries.name: Lump of labour fallacy
entries.definition: Treating the total amount of work in an economy as fixed, so that every job taken by one person or machine must be a job lost by another.
entries.example: If older people work longer, there will be fewer jobs for the young.
required_conditions: The total amount of work is assumed to be fixed.
It is concluded that a job taken by one person or machine is a job lost by another.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A specific, local displacement where fixed demand is shown.

entries.name: Magical thinking
entries.definition: Assuming a causal link between events that have no plausible connection, such as between thoughts, rituals or symbols and outside events.
entries.example: If I think about the accident, it might happen.
required_conditions: A causal link is claimed between thoughts, words, rituals or symbols and outside events.
There is no plausible mechanism, and the conclusion relies on the link.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Rituals valued for their psychological effect on the person doing them.
If the reasoning is only 'it followed, so it caused', use post hoc.

entries.name: McNamara fallacy
entries.definition: Deciding only on what can easily be measured and treating what can't be measured as unimportant or nonexistent.
entries.example: Test scores went up, so the school is better, never mind whether students learn to think.
required_conditions: A decision or judgement is based on measured quantities.
Something important to the goal is not captured by those measures.
It is ignored or dismissed because it is hard to measure.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The measured thing is the thing that matters.

entries.name: Middle ground
entries.definition: Taking it for granted that the truth must lie halfway between two opposing positions.
entries.example: You say the bridge needs 10 tonnes of steel; he says 2. Let's use 6.
required_conditions: Two positions are in dispute.
The midpoint is asserted to be correct, fair, safe or true, not merely offered as a settlement.
Its being in the middle is the only reason given. (A midpoint that carries a factual claim, such as that it is safe or affordable, needs evidence for that claim.)

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The midpoint is offered as a settlement both sides can accept ('let's settle at 4%').
The midpoint is backed by independent evidence (audits, data), not only by being in the middle.

entries.name: Mind projection fallacy
entries.definition: Treating a feature of how we perceive or know something as if it were a property of the thing itself.
entries.example: The coin toss is random, so randomness is a physical property of the coin.
required_conditions: A feature of how something is perceived or known (such as uncertainty or taste) is identified.
It is attributed to the thing itself.
A conclusion depends on that attribution.

entries.name: Misleading vividness
entries.definition: Letting a few dramatic, memorable cases outweigh a larger body of statistical evidence.
entries.example: I saw a terrible shark attack on the news, so swimming at the beach is too dangerous, whatever the statistics say.
required_conditions: A vivid, memorable case is described.
It is used to support a claim about how common or likely something is.
Statistical evidence pointing the other way exists (stated, or well known) and is outweighed or ignored.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A vivid case used as an illustration of a pattern shown by the statistics.
Pick one of misleading vividness or anecdotal evidence for a given step.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)

entries.name: Misplaced burden of proof
entries.definition: Demanding that others prove you wrong when it is your job to support your own claim.
entries.example: I say this herb cures colds. Prove it doesn't.
required_conditions: A claim is made.
The person making it says others must disprove it.
The claimant has given no support.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Asking for proof is proper; asking someone to support their own claim is not this fallacy.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misplaced Burden of Proof"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: After a real case has been made, asking the other side for its case is fair.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misplaced Burden of Proof"

entries.name: Modal scope fallacy
entries.definition: Treating 'necessarily, if P then Q' as if it were 'if P, then necessarily Q', so that a merely true conclusion is wrongly presented as a necessary one.
entries.example: Necessarily, if you are married you have a spouse. You are married. So you necessarily have a spouse (as if you could not have stayed single).
required_conditions: A premise of the form 'necessarily, if P then Q' (or a conditional that is true by definition) is used.
P is merely true, not necessary.
Q is concluded to be necessary.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: P itself is shown to be necessary, in which case Q is necessary too.

sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Modal scope fallacy"

entries.name: Moralistic fallacy
entries.definition: Inferring what is the case from what ought to be the case, for example concluding that something can't be true because it would be bad if it were.
entries.example: People shouldn't be unequal in ability, so there are no differences in ability.
required_conditions: A factual question is at issue.
A claim about what ought to be is used to conclude what is the case.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A moral claim used only as a reason to check the evidence carefully.

entries.name: Motte-and-bailey
entries.definition: Defending a bold, controversial claim by retreating to a modest, easy-to-defend claim when challenged, then returning to the bold claim once the challenge passes.
entries.example: 'Medicine is a scam.' Challenged: 'I just mean drug companies sometimes put profit first.'
required_conditions: A bold, contested claim is put forward (the 'bailey').
When challenged, the speaker defends only a modest, easily defended claim (the 'motte').
The bold claim is then resumed or treated as vindicated.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Different people in a movement holding bold and modest versions (no single speaker switching).
Openly retreating to the modest claim and leaving the bold one aside.

entries.name: Moving the goalposts
entries.definition: Demanding new or greater evidence once the evidence originally asked for has been supplied.
entries.example: You showed me one study? Show me ten. Ten? They must be from other countries.
required_conditions: A standard of evidence or success is stated.
It is met (or the evidence is supplied).
A new, stricter standard is then demanded, and the stated reason (if any) is neither new information nor a change in the claim, so it would already have applied when the first standard was set.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Raising the standard because of something learned after it was set (for example, a flaw in how it was met), or because the claim has grown.

entries.name: Multiple comparisons fallacy
entries.definition: Making many comparisons in one set of data and then treating a 'significant' result as meaningful, without allowing for the fact that some will turn up by chance.
entries.example: We checked 40 foods against 40 diseases and found that eating celery is linked to ear infections.
required_conditions: Many comparisons or tests were made on the data.
One or a few 'significant' results are reported as meaningful.
No allowance is made for the number of comparisons.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Results are corrected for multiple comparisons or confirmed in new data.

entries.name: Naturalistic fallacy
entries.definition: Defining 'good' as identical to some natural property (such as pleasure, what is desired, or what evolved) and treating the matter as settled. Sources also use the name for any move from 'is' to 'ought' and for 'natural, so good'; use is-ought or appeal to nature for those.
entries.example: Pleasure is what people desire, so pleasure is what is good.
required_conditions: 'Good' (or another value term) is defined as, or treated as identical to, some natural property.
The identity is treated as settled, without argument.
A value conclusion is drawn from it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Arguing (not assuming) that some natural property is a reliable sign of goodness.
If the error is a bare step from 'is' to 'ought', use is-ought; if it is 'natural, so good', use appeal to nature.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Naturalistic fallacy"

entries.name: Naturalistic fallacy fallacy
entries.definition: Rejecting any argument from facts to values as a naturalistic fallacy even when it supplies the value premises needed to make it work.
entries.example: You can't argue that smoking is bad because it causes cancer. That's deriving an ought from an is!
required_conditions: An argument moves from facts to a value conclusion.
It supplies (or plainly assumes) the value premise needed.
It is rejected as a naturalistic fallacy anyway.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Relevance fallacies > Red herring fallacies", item "Naturalistic fallacy fallacy"

entries.name: Negative conclusion from affirmative premises
entries.definition: A syllogism with only affirmative premises but a negative conclusion.
entries.example: All pets are tame. Some birds are pets. So some birds are not tame.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism.
Both premises are affirmative.
The conclusion is negative.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Formal fallacies > Syllogistic fallacies", item "Negative conclusion from affirmative premises"

entries.name: Nirvana fallacy
entries.definition: Rejecting a solution because it isn't perfect, rather than comparing it with realistic alternatives.
entries.example: Seatbelts don't prevent all deaths, so there's no point wearing them.
required_conditions: A proposal or solution is criticised.
The criticism is that it is imperfect or doesn't solve the whole problem.
It is rejected without comparing it with realistic alternatives.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The situation requires perfection or near-perfection (for example, some safety standards).

entries.name: No true Scotsman
entries.definition: Protecting a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group so that the counterexample doesn't count.
entries.example: No true environmentalist flies. She flies? Then she's not a true environmentalist.
required_conditions: A general claim about a group is made.
A counterexample is offered.
The counterexample is excluded by redefining the group on the spot, with no independent criterion.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Excluding a case using a criterion stated beforehand or independently justified.
Applying a criterion that is part of what the word means (someone who eats meat is not a vegan).

entries.name: Non-cause (Aristotle's sense)
entries.definition: In an argument that derives an absurdity from several assumptions, blaming the absurdity on an assumption that played no part in deriving it and rejecting that assumption. This is different from the modern false cause fallacy about real-world causes.
entries.example: From A, B and C we derived a contradiction, so C must be false (though the contradiction follows from A and B alone).
required_conditions: An argument derives an impossible or false result from several premises (a reduction to absurdity).
One premise is blamed and rejected.
The premise blamed was not needed to derive the result.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The blamed premise was in fact used in deriving the result.
For real-world causal errors, use false cause.

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: Non sequitur
entries.definition: A conclusion that doesn't follow from the reasons given, because they are irrelevant to it or far too weak.
entries.example: She's an excellent cook, so she'll make a fine senator.
required_conditions: A conclusion is drawn from stated reasons.
The reasons are irrelevant to it or extremely weak (state the missing link).
No more specific named entry describes the defect.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An invalid argument that still has real inductive strength (for example, affirming the consequent with good evidence) is not a non sequitur.

source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Non Sequitur"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An enthymeme whose unstated premise is obvious and acceptable.
If the step has a named invalid form, or you can show a same-form counterexample, use that entry or formal fallacy; do not tag both.

entries.name: Nut-picking
entries.definition: Finding the most extreme or fringe members of an opposing group and presenting them as typical of the whole group.
entries.example: Look at this one ranting post; that's what all supporters of that policy are like.
required_conditions: Statements by a group's most extreme members are cited.
They are presented as representing the whole group.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Examples that are shown to be typical.

entries.name: Obscurum per obscurius
aliases: explaining the obscure by the more obscure
entries.definition: Explaining something unclear by appeal to something even less clear.
entries.example: Consciousness is just the quantum vibration of universal mind.
required_conditions: Something is offered as an explanation or definition.
The explanation uses terms less clear than the thing explained.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Technical terms used for a specialist audience that knows them.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Obscurum per Obscurius"

entries.name: Observational interpretation fallacy
entries.definition: Reading an association found in an observational study as proof of cause and effect.
entries.example: People who drink coffee in this survey live longer, so coffee extends life.
required_conditions: The evidence is an association from an observational study (not a controlled experiment).
A causal conclusion is drawn.
Confounders or reverse causation are not adequately addressed, and the causal claim is stated as established.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The association is reported as a link to be tested, or confounders are carefully controlled.
Partial adjustment for confounders with a hedged causal claim: record possible issue and name the alternative left unaddressed.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Observational interpretation fallacy"

entries.name: Over-extrapolation
entries.definition: Extending a trend far beyond the range of data that support it, as if it would continue indefinitely.
entries.example: The child grew 8 cm this year, so by age 40 he'll be over 4 metres tall.
required_conditions: A trend is observed over some range.
It is extended far beyond that range.
No reason is given to think the trend continues there.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Short-range forecasts with stated uncertainty, or extrapolation backed by a model of why the trend continues.

entries.name: Overgenerality
entries.definition: Using a concept or claim so broad that it gives no useful information in context, often to avoid committing to anything checkable.
entries.example: My plan for the economy is to make things better for people.
required_conditions: A claim is stated in terms so broad it rules nothing out in context.
It is offered as if it answered a more specific question.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A deliberately general summary that is not offered as a specific answer.
If the fault is a broad generalization from too little evidence, use hasty generalization.

entries.name: Oversimplification
entries.definition: Leaving out relevant complexity when the omitted complexity would weaken the conclusion, so that the simple version is what makes the conclusion look supported.
entries.example: Crime is down because we hired more police. That's all there is to it.
required_conditions: A complex matter is described simply.
The left-out factor is relevant (name it).
Including it would weaken the conclusion.
No more specific entry (single cause, false dilemma) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Simplification for clarity that does not change the conclusion.

entries.name: Overwhelming exception
entries.definition: A generalization stated with so many qualifications that what is left is much weaker than the headline claim suggests.
entries.example: All our customers are satisfied, apart from those who complained, returned the product, or didn't respond.
required_conditions: A general claim is made.
It is qualified with so many exceptions that little is left.
It is still presented as the strong headline claim.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Faulty generalizations", item "Overwhelming exception"

entries.name: P-hacking
entries.definition: Trying many analyses or experiments and reporting only the ones that cross the significance threshold, so the reported result looks stronger than it is.
entries.example: We ran twenty versions of the study and published the one that reached p < 0.05.
required_conditions: Several analyses, versions or experiments were run.
Only those reaching the significance threshold are reported.
The reported result is presented as if it were the only test.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: All analyses are reported, or the analysis was registered in advance.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "p-hacking"

entries.name: Package deal
entries.definition: Treating essentially different concepts as though they were essentially the same, usually because they are commonly grouped together.
entries.example: Criticising a government policy is the same as hating the country.
required_conditions: Two or more concepts are treated as one.
They differ in an essential respect (state it).
The conclusion relies on treating them as the same.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Grouping things that really do share the relevant feature.

entries.name: Pathetic fallacy
entries.definition: Holding a mistaken belief because you attribute human feelings or purposes to inanimate things.
entries.example: The storm is angry at us for building on this coast.
required_conditions: Feelings or intentions are attributed to inanimate nature.
A conclusion relies on the attribution being literal.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Figurative description in literature.
Do not also tag anthropomorphism.

entries.name: Persuasive definition
entries.definition: Winning an argument by getting others to accept a slanted definition of a key term that builds in the desired conclusion.
entries.example: Real art means beautiful art, so this abstract painting isn't real art.
required_conditions: A term is defined, or its use is narrowed or stretched, in a way that differs from its ordinary meaning.
The definition builds in a contested evaluation or conclusion.
The definition is presented as neutral, and the argument depends on it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A stipulated technical definition that is announced and used consistently.
Arguing openly for a revised definition.

entries.name: Poisoning the well
entries.definition: Discrediting a person in advance, before they speak, so that anything they say will be dismissed.
entries.example: Before you hear from my opponent, remember that he's a paid lobbyist who'll say anything.
required_conditions: Before a person speaks or presents a case, negative information about them is offered.
The information is presented so that whatever they say will be discounted.
It is irrelevant to the merits of what they will argue, or is used to dismiss it wholesale.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Disclosing a documented conflict of interest relevant to testimony, while still weighing the argument on its merits.

entries.name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
aliases: after this, therefore because of this
entries.definition: Concluding that because B happened after A, A caused B.
entries.example: I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks helped us win.
required_conditions: One event followed another.
The first is concluded to have caused the second.
The order in time is the main or only evidence offered.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Sequence is some evidence of cause; the fallacy is the hasty leap, not considering timing.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Timing plus a known mechanism or controlled comparison.

entries.name: Proof by assertion
entries.definition: Restating a claim again and again despite objections or contrary evidence, without answering them, as if restating it settled the matter.
entries.example: This diet works. It works. I've told you a hundred times: it works.
required_conditions: A claim is contested or a counterargument is offered.
The claim is asserted again as settled.
The contradiction or counterargument is not addressed.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Briefly maintaining a position while promising or citing an answer elsewhere.
If others' silence or the number of repetitions is itself cited as evidence, use argument from repetition instead.

entries.name: Proof surrogate
entries.definition: Substituting a phrase that suggests proof, such as 'everyone knows' or 'studies show', for actual evidence.
entries.example: Any reasonable person can see the plan is sound, and experts agree.
required_conditions: A claim is made.
A phrase suggesting proof ('studies show', 'everyone knows') is used.
No actual evidence is given or identified.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The phrase is accompanied by a checkable citation.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Proof Surrogate"

entries.name: Prosecutor's fallacy
entries.definition: Confusing the chance of the evidence given innocence with the chance of innocence given the evidence, which overstates how strongly evidence points to guilt.
entries.example: Only 1 in a million people would match this blood type, so there is only a 1 in a million chance the defendant is innocent.
required_conditions: The probability of the evidence given innocence (or given some hypothesis) is stated.
It is presented as the probability of innocence (or of the hypothesis) given the evidence.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The base rate and other evidence are combined correctly to estimate the probability of guilt.
If the error is ignoring how common the condition is when reading a test or screening result, use base-rate fallacy.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Prosecutor's Fallacy"

entries.name: Proving too much
entries.definition: An argument that leads to an overly general conclusion. A common test (this catalog's wording, not the cited source's): the same reasoning would also establish things the arguer would reject.
entries.example: We shouldn't fund the new library because some people never read (the same reasoning would rule out funding anything some people don't use).
required_conditions: An argument for a conclusion is given.
The same reasoning applies to cases where it yields a conclusion the arguer would reject (give one).
No relevant difference blocks that application.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A relevant difference between the cases is stated.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"
sources.note: Wikipedia describes it only as an argument that results in an overly generalized conclusion; the 'would also prove things the arguer rejects' test is catalog wording

entries.name: Psychologist's fallacy
entries.definition: An observer assumes their own perspective is objective and reads it into the behaviour or experience they are studying.
entries.example: I would have felt humiliated in that situation, so the subject must have felt humiliated.
required_conditions: An observer describes someone else's experience or reasoning.
The observer's own perspective is attributed to the person observed.
A conclusion depends on the attribution.

entries.name: Quantifier shift
entries.definition: Swapping the order of 'every' and 'some': moving from 'everything has some X' to 'there is one X that everything has'.
entries.example: Every child has a mother. So there is one woman who is the mother of every child.
required_conditions: A premise says that for every X there is some Y (each X has its own Y).
The conclusion says there is one Y that goes with every X.
Nothing else supports the single shared Y.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Separate evidence shows that a single shared Y exists.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Quantifier Shift"

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Every and All"

entries.name: Question-begging analogy
entries.definition: An argument by analogy whose force depends on the very point in dispute.
entries.example: Eating meat is like eating people, so it's wrong.
required_conditions: An analogy is offered.
Whether the two cases are alike in the relevant respect is the very point in dispute.
The analogy is used to settle that point.

entries.name: Quibbling
entries.definition: Complaining about a minor point as if that undermined the whole argument.
entries.example: You wrote 'less' instead of 'fewer', so your argument about the budget is worthless.
required_conditions: An objection targets a minor point.
The point does not affect the main argument.
The objection is presented as undermining the whole argument.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Correcting a minor error without claiming it defeats the argument.

entries.name: Quoting out of context
entries.definition: Quoting someone selectively so that the context that fixes their meaning is lost and they appear to say something else.
entries.example: The critic called the film 'a triumph ... of marketing over substance', and the poster says 'a triumph!'.
required_conditions: Someone's words are quoted or paraphrased.
Surrounding words that change the meaning are left out (quote the fuller original; without it, at most possible issue).
The argument relies on the shifted meaning.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A shortened quote that keeps the original meaning.

entries.name: Rationalization
entries.definition: Offering reasons that are not the real reasons for a belief or action, chosen to make it look more acceptable.
entries.example: I bought the sports car for its safety rating.
required_conditions: A reason is given for an action or belief.
The stated reason is not the actual reason.
The real reason is hidden.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A reason that may have come after the fact but is still sound; judge the reason on its merits.
Do not flag from the text alone; it needs independent evidence that the stated reason was not the real one.

entries.name: Red herring
entries.definition: Bringing in an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the issue under discussion.
entries.example: Why worry about the factory's pollution when so many people need jobs?
required_conditions: An issue is under discussion.
A different topic is introduced.
The new topic does not bear on the issue and draws attention away from it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A related point that is shown to bear on the issue.
Arguing that another issue must be settled first, when that dependence is real.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Avoiding the Issue"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Merely asserting that another question must be settled first does not count; the dependence must be shown.
Asking that a stated test be applied consistently is legitimate, unless it is used to dismiss the original criticism.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Red Herring"

entries.name: Redefinition
entries.definition: Giving a familiar term a new meaning and then slipping between the new and the ordinary meanings in the course of an argument.
entries.example: Counting everyone under 25 as 'youth', youth unemployment is high, so teenagers can't find summer jobs.
required_conditions: A word is used with a meaning different from its usual one.
The shift is not announced.
The argument trades on the usual meaning's associations or implications.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Announced, consistent technical usage.

entries.name: Reductio ad Hitlerum
entries.definition: A form of guilt by association: discrediting a view because Hitler or the Nazis held it or something like it.
entries.example: Hitler was a vegetarian, so vegetarianism is suspect.
required_conditions: A view or person is compared to or linked with Hitler or the Nazis.
The link is offered as a reason to reject the view.
The shared feature is not what made the Nazis wrong.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A historical comparison where the shared feature is the morally relevant one and this is argued.

entries.name: Referential fallacy
entries.definition: Assuming that every word refers to a real thing and that a word's meaning is just the thing it refers to.
entries.example: We have a word for 'luck', so luck must be a force in the world.
required_conditions: A word is assumed to name a real thing because the word exists, or its meaning is taken to be just its referent.
A conclusion relies on that assumption.

entries.name: Regression fallacy
entries.definition: Crediting a cause for a change that is just extreme results drifting back toward the average.
entries.example: After her worst game of the season she wore a new bracelet, and next game she played better. The bracelet works.
required_conditions: An unusually extreme result was followed by a more ordinary one.
Something done in between is credited with causing the change.
Drift back toward the average is not considered.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A comparison group that also started extreme shows less change, so the effect exceeds regression.

sources.locator: section "Informal fallacies > Questionable cause > Statistical fallacies", item "Regression fallacy"

entries.name: Reification
entries.definition: Treating an abstraction, such as 'society', 'nature' or 'the market', as if it were a concrete thing or agent with its own will.
entries.example: The market wants lower interest rates, so the central bank should obey it.
required_conditions: An abstraction (society, the market, nature) is described as acting, wanting or deciding.
The argument draws a conclusion that depends on taking that literally.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Figurative use in poetry, or shorthand that is not relied on to reach a conclusion.
Shorthand for the actions of real people when it can be unpacked without changing the conclusion.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Misplaced Concreteness"

entries.name: Relative privation
entries.definition: Dismissing a problem or complaint because worse problems exist elsewhere.
entries.example: Why complain about potholes when people in other countries have no roads?
required_conditions: A problem or complaint is raised.
Worse problems elsewhere are cited.
This is offered as a reason to dismiss or ignore the problem raised.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Comparing problems when the actual question is how to rank priorities.

entries.name: Retrospective determinism
entries.definition: Assuming that because something happened under certain circumstances, those circumstances made it inevitable.
entries.example: The company collapsed, so its collapse was bound to happen from the day it was founded.
required_conditions: Something happened under certain circumstances.
It is concluded that those circumstances made it inevitable.
No reason is given why it could not have turned out otherwise.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A demonstrated mechanism that left no alternative.

entries.name: Reversing causation
entries.definition: Getting cause and effect the wrong way round.
entries.example: Hospitals are full of sick people, so hospitals make people sick.
required_conditions: A link between A and B is observed.
A is concluded to cause B.
B plausibly causes A instead, and this is not addressed.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Two-way causation, or a reverse direction ruled out by timing or design.

sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Reversing Causation"

entries.name: Scapegoating
entries.definition: Blaming a person or group for a problem without evidence of their role, relying on their already being disliked or unpopular.
entries.example: Sales are down because of those newcomers from the city. Everyone here knows what they're like.
required_conditions: A problem is blamed on a person or group.
No evidence of their role is given.
The blame relies on their already being disliked or unpopular.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Blame backed by evidence, however unpopular the target.

entries.name: Scope fallacy
entries.definition: Misreading or shifting how much of a sentence a word like 'not', 'all' or 'necessarily' applies to, and drawing a conclusion from the wrong reading.
entries.example: 'Everyone isn't coming' means no one is coming, so the party is cancelled (when the speaker meant 'not everyone is coming').
required_conditions: A sentence contains a word such as 'not', 'all', 'every' or 'necessarily' whose reach is ambiguous.
The argument relies on one reading.
The conclusion fails on the reading the speaker most plausibly meant.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Only one reading is plausible in context.

entries.name: Secundum quid
aliases: a dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter
entries.definition: Aristotle's fallacy of treating something true only in a certain respect, or with a qualification, as if it were true without qualification.
entries.example: He's a good thief, and someone who is good is a good person, so he is a good person.
required_conditions: A claim is true only in some respect, at some time or with some qualification.
It is used as if it were true without qualification.
The conclusion relies on dropping the qualification.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The qualification does not affect the conclusion.
A rule applied to a genuine exception is accident; too few cases is hasty generalization.

sources.title: Aristotle, On Sophistical Refutations, trans. W. A. Pickard-Cambridge (Internet Classics Archive)

entries.name: Selective attention
entries.definition: Focusing on some aspects of a situation while ignoring others that are relevant.
entries.example: 'How was school?' 'I got an A in art!' (the four failed tests go unmentioned).
required_conditions: A conclusion is drawn from observations.
Only observations fitting an expectation were noticed.
Contrary observations were available.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: If the text omits known contrary evidence, consider suppressed evidence.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Selective Attention"

entries.name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
entries.definition: Treating the fulfilment of a prediction as confirming it, when the act of predicting helped bring the outcome about.
entries.example: I told everyone the bank would fail; the run on the bank proved me right.
required_conditions: A prediction is made.
Making or acting on it helped bring it about.
Its coming true is cited as proof that it was right independently.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy"

entries.name: Fallacy of the single cause
entries.definition: Assuming an outcome has one simple cause when it actually arose from several causes acting together.
entries.example: The war started because an archduke was shot.
required_conditions: An outcome is attributed to one cause.
Other contributing causes are known or evident (name one).
The conclusion relies on the single cause being the whole story.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Picking out the most important or most controllable cause while acknowledging others.

entries.name: Slippery slope
entries.definition: Claiming that a first step will lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without good reason to think each step will actually follow.
entries.example: If we let students redo one test, soon they'll expect to redo every test, and degrees will be worthless.
required_conditions: A first step is opposed.
It is claimed to lead through a chain of steps to an undesirable result.

At least one step in the chain is given no adequate reason to think it likely. Evidence for the first link does not support later links, and a hedge ('probably') lowers the claimed probability but does not supply a missing link.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Whether this is fallacious depends on how likely each step is; well-supported chains are reasonable.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Slippery Slope"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A chain of tiny vague steps with no practical prediction is line-drawing, not this.

When each later step needs a new decision by the same body, that step is not likely unless a binding mechanism (a precedent rule, a legal duty, bylaws) is shown. If one is shown, the step is supported.

entries.name: Smokescreen
entries.definition: Offering so many details or side issues that the main point, or the evidence against it, is obscured.
entries.example: Responding to one question about safety with a 40-page technical appendix nobody can parse.
required_conditions: A point is challenged.
The response offers many details or side issues.
These obscure the main point or the evidence against it.
No more specific entry (red herring, logic-chopping) fits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Raising reasonable cautions or complexity that actually bear on the point.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: If the detail hides counterevidence, use suppressed evidence; if it changes the subject, use red herring.

entries.name: Some are / some are not
entries.definition: Inferring 'Some A are not B' from 'Some A are B', or the reverse. 'Some' does not logically mean 'not all'.
entries.example: Some of the samples are contaminated, so some of them are clean.
required_conditions: 'Some A are B' (or 'Some A are not B') is accepted.
'Some A are not B' (or 'Some A are B') is concluded from it alone, as a matter of logic.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Reading 'some' as a conversational hint of 'not all' when the speaker plainly meant it that way.

source.title: The Fallacy Files (Gary N. Curtis)
source.locator: entry "Some Are/Some Are Not"

entries.name: Special pleading
entries.definition: Applying a rule or standard to others while exempting yourself or a favoured case without justifying the exception.
entries.example: Everyone should obey the speed limit, but I'm a good driver, so I can go faster.
required_conditions: A general rule or standard is accepted.
An exception is claimed for one case.
No reason relevant to the rule's purpose is given for the exception; rank, convenience or 'I'm busy' do not count.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A relevant difference is stated and supported.

sources.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
sources.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Special Pleading"

entries.name: Specificity
entries.definition: Drawing a more specific conclusion than the evidence supports.
entries.example: The trails were dug by an animal, so a badger dug them last Tuesday night.
required_conditions: A conclusion is drawn.
It is more specific than the evidence supports (for example, naming one cause when evidence only shows some cause).

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Do not also tag jumping to conclusions.

entries.name: Stereotyping
entries.definition: Applying a group image to an individual member, or to every member, as if it were a reliable rule, without evidence about that individual.
entries.example: She's an accountant, so she must be boring.
required_conditions: A trait is attributed to a group.
It is applied to an individual member.
The individual's own characteristics are not considered, or the group claim lacks adequate evidence.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Reasoning from well-supported group rates to a probability, when no individual information is available, and stating it as a probability.

entries.name: Straw man
entries.definition: Misrepresenting someone's position as a weaker or more extreme version and then attacking that version instead of what they actually hold.
entries.example: She wants stricter emissions rules. So she wants to ban cars and make us all ride bicycles.
required_conditions: The opponent's position is restated or summarised.
The restatement differs materially from what they said or meant (show the original wording or a reliable summary of it; without it, at most possible issue).
The argument attacks the restatement.
The attack is presented as refuting the opponent's actual position.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Restating a view in words its holder would accept.
Drawing out a consequence the opponent is actually committed to.
Rebutting a version of the view that someone really holds, while saying whose version it is.

entries.name: Style over substance
entries.definition: Treating the polish, confidence or catchiness of how an argument is delivered as if it added to how strong the argument is.
entries.example: Vote for Ray, he will save the day! (a slogan offered in place of a reason to prefer him)
required_conditions: An argument or position is presented with notable polish, confidence, rhyme or charm.
The presentation is treated as a reason to accept it, in place of support.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Clear, persuasive presentation of a well-supported case.

entries.name: Subjectivist fallacy
aliases: true for you, not for me
entries.definition: Rejecting a claim on the grounds that truth is just a matter of opinion, when the claim is about objective fact.
entries.example: Maybe the earth is round for you, but that's not my truth.
required_conditions: A claim about a matter of fact is offered with reasons.
It is rejected on the ground that truth is relative to the person ('true for you, not for me').

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Claims that really are about personal taste or preference.
If the reply is only that one has a right to an opinion, use entitled to my opinion.

entries.name: Sunk cost fallacy
entries.definition: Continuing with something because of what has already been spent on it, rather than judging it on its future costs and benefits.
entries.example: We've already spent two years on this failing project, so we have to keep going.
required_conditions: A choice about what to do next is being made.
Past costs that cannot be recovered are cited.
They are treated as a reason to continue, independent of future costs and benefits.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Past investment as evidence about future prospects (for example, the project is nearly done).
Keeping a commitment for reasons of trust or reputation.
A real remaining benefit, or a real cost of switching, can be a reason to continue.

entries.name: Superstitious thinking
entries.definition: Treating omens, charms, rituals or similar grounds that are well known to be unreliable as reasons for a belief or as causes of events.
entries.example: A black cat crossed my path, so I'll cancel the interview.
required_conditions: A belief or prediction rests on omens, charms or similar grounds.
Those grounds are well known to be unreliable.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: If the reasoning is 'it followed, so it caused', use post hoc; if it claims thoughts or rituals act on the world, use magical thinking.

entries.name: Suppressed correlative
entries.definition: Redefining one of a pair of contrasting terms so that the other has nothing left to apply to.
entries.example: I'm not fat; John is fatter than me, so only John counts as fat.
required_conditions: A pair of contrasting terms is in play.
One term is redefined to cover everything.
The other is left with nothing to apply to, and the argument relies on this.

entries.name: Suppressed evidence
entries.definition: Leaving out evidence that is significant and would weaken the conclusion, when the arguer had it or should have had it, and presenting the case as if it were complete.
entries.example: Our drug helped 30 patients (we won't mention the 70 it didn't).
required_conditions: An argument presents evidence for a conclusion.
Relevant, significant evidence against it is omitted (identify it).
The arguer knew or should have known of it.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The omitted evidence is not significant, or the arguer could not have known it.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Suppressed Evidence"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: An openly one-sided brief in an adversarial setting where the other side presents its case.
A short case that does not claim to be complete.
If the contrary evidence is stated in the passage (or plainly known) and simply ignored, use cherry-picking.

entries.name: Survivorship bias
entries.definition: Drawing conclusions from the cases that made it through some filter while ignoring the ones that didn't.
entries.example: All the famous dropouts became billionaires, so dropping out is a good career move.
required_conditions: The evidence consists only of cases that passed some filter (survived, succeeded, were published).
The cases that did not pass are relevant and ignored.
A general conclusion is drawn.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The question is only about the survivors themselves.
If the filter is how the sample was gathered, use unrepresentative sample; use this only when the filtered-out cases are the missing ones.

entries.name: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
entries.definition: Picking out a cluster or pattern after looking at the data, then treating it as meaningful as if it had been predicted beforehand (like painting a target around bullet holes).
entries.example: Five people on this street got sick, so something on this street is causing it (out of thousands of streets, some will have clusters by chance).
required_conditions: A cluster or pattern is picked out after looking at the data.
It is treated as meaningful or as evidence of a cause.
No allowance is made for how many patterns could have been found by chance, and no prior prediction was made.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The pattern was predicted before the data were examined.
A cluster found by searching is treated only as a lead to test with new data.
If the arguer just picks the favourable part of data already on the table, with no pattern-search, use cherry-picking.

entries.name: Thought-terminating cliché
entries.definition: Using a stock phrase to end discussion rather than to answer the point.
entries.example: It is what it is.
required_conditions: A question or doubt is raised.
A stock phrase ('it is what it is', 'everything happens for a reason') is offered.
The phrase is used to end discussion rather than answer.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The phrase sums up a reason that has been given.

entries.name: Tokenism
entries.definition: Accepting a token gesture as if it were an adequate substitute for real action.
entries.example: The company planted ten trees, so it clearly cares about the environment.
required_conditions: A gesture or small step is offered.
It is presented as an adequate response to a problem.
It is clearly inadequate to the problem.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A small step openly offered as a first step.

entries.name: Tone policing
entries.definition: Dismissing an argument because of the emotion or manner in which it is delivered rather than its content.
entries.example: I'll listen to your complaint once you calm down.
required_conditions: Someone raises a point in an emotional or forceful manner.
The manner is offered as a reason to reject or ignore the point.
The point itself is not answered.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Objecting to threats or abuse while still answering the point.
Asking for a calmer tone as a condition of conversation, without claiming the point is wrong.

entries.name: Traitorous critic fallacy
aliases: if you don't like it, leave
entries.definition: Answering criticism by attacking the critic's loyalty and telling them to leave, instead of addressing the criticism.
entries.example: If you hate this country's healthcare so much, move somewhere else.
required_conditions: Someone criticises a group, place or institution they belong to.
The reply questions their loyalty or tells them to leave.
The criticism itself is not answered.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "List of fallacies"

entries.name: Tu quoque
entries.definition: Dismissing a claim or criticism because the person making it doesn't live up to it themselves.
entries.example: You say smoking is bad for me, but you smoke.
required_conditions: Someone makes a claim or criticism.

The reply points out that they do not act consistently with it, and the inconsistency concerns the same claim or the principle directly behind it. (If it is looser, such as being overweight while urging someone to quit smoking, use ad hominem.)
This is offered as a reason the claim or criticism is false or can be dismissed.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Finding that a speaker is a hypocrite gives reason to be suspicious of their reasoning, but not enough reason to discount it.

source.title: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Fallacies" (Bradley Dowden)
source.locator: section 6, "Partial List of Fallacies", entry "Tu Quoque"

legitimate_lookalikes.text: If the reply targets the person's sincerity or fitness for a role, that is this look-alike; if it targets the message or policy, flag.
'What about X?' that changes the subject to a third party is not this; consider red herring.
'Whataboutism' is not a reliable alias: only the 'you do it too, so your point fails' form is this fallacy.

entries.name: Two wrongs make a right
entries.definition: Defending a wrong action because someone else did something wrong, as if one wrong cancels another.
entries.example: He cheated on the last test, so it's fine for me to cheat on this one.
required_conditions: An action is admitted or alleged to be wrong.
Someone else's wrongdoing is cited.
That is offered as making the action right or acceptable.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Arguing that a rule is enforced unevenly, or about what penalty is fair, rather than that the act was right.
Proportionate self-defence or restitution argued on its own terms.
If a criticism is dismissed because the critic does the same, use tu quoque.

entries.name: Undistributed middle
entries.definition: A categorical syllogism in which the middle term (the one shared by both premises) never covers all members of its class, so the premises fail to link the other two terms.
entries.example: All spies wear sunglasses. My neighbor wears sunglasses. So my neighbor is a spy.
required_conditions: The argument is a categorical syllogism (two premises sharing a middle term).
In neither premise does the middle term refer to all members of its class.
A conclusion linking the other two terms is drawn.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A probabilistic argument ('most spies wear sunglasses...') offered as mere evidence, not proof.

entries.name: Unfalsifiability
entries.definition: Offering an explanation of events that no possible observation could count against, and treating that as a strength of the explanation.
entries.example: The cure works for those with enough faith; if it didn't work for you, your faith was too weak.
required_conditions: A claim is offered as an empirical claim about the world.
It is framed so that no possible observation could count against it.
It is still presented as established or explanatory, although its framing, not evidence, is what protects it from refutation.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Definitions, mathematics, logical truths and value claims, which are not offered as explanations of events.

entries.name: Unrepresentative sample
entries.definition: Generalizing about a population from a sample that was gathered in a way likely to differ from that population. Self-selection, where people choose whether to take part, is a common cause.
entries.example: Our website poll shows 80% of people love our product.
required_conditions: A conclusion about a population is drawn from a sample.
The way the sample was gathered is likely to make it differ from the population (for example, people chose to take part).
The difference bears on the conclusion.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: The sample is limited but the conclusion is limited to match.
Biased-looking samples that have been weighted or checked against the population.

entries.name: Vacuous truth (misuse)
entries.definition: Offering a claim that is technically true only because there is nothing for it to be about, as if it were informative.
entries.example: None of our cars have ever failed a safety test (we've never had one tested).
required_conditions: A universal claim is offered as informative.
It is true only because the class it is about is empty.

entries.name: Vagueness (exploiting)
entries.definition: Relying on a word with fuzzy boundaries so that a claim can't be tested or pinned down, or so that it seems to cover more than it does.
entries.example: This supplement supports wellness.
required_conditions: A key term in the argument has no clear boundaries in this context.
The conclusion depends on how the term is read.
The vagueness is used to avoid checking or to shift meanings.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: A vague term is not hopelessly vague; vagueness that does not affect the conclusion is harmless.

entries.name: Willed ignorance
entries.definition: Openly refusing to look at, or respond to, evidence or arguments against a view one has already decided to hold.
entries.example: I've decided the treatment works, and I'm not reading any more studies about it.
required_conditions: A view is held.
Counterevidence or arguments are pointed out.
The speaker openly refuses to look at or respond to them.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Declining to revisit something already thoroughly considered, with a reason.
Remaining unconvinced after looking at the evidence.

entries.name: Wishful thinking
entries.definition: Believing or rejecting a claim because of how much you want it to be so, rather than because of evidence.
entries.example: The tumour must be benign. I can't bear to think otherwise.
required_conditions: A claim is accepted or rejected.
The stated or evident reason is that the speaker wants it to be true (or false).
No evidence is offered.

legitimate_lookalikes.text: Hope as a motive for action rather than a reason for belief.
